meta.legal: This guide was prepared by [John Guerrero](https://johnguerrero.es) for AI Chef Pro as a practical reference for restaurant, bar, cafe, bakery, catering and food truck operators. It is not legal, tax, employment or food safety advice. Rules change and they vary by state, province, territory, county, city and council: before you print a menu, sign a contract, run payroll or open your doors, check every figure with the official source listed in section 10, your accountant or your local authority. The legal figures in this guide were checked against official government sources in October 2026.
meta.contents_note: How to read the tables: the first column says what the thing is; the next four columns give the word or the rule in the US, the UK, Canada and Australia. Local words appear in quotation marks.

sections.h1: 1. How to Use This Guide with Your Kit

blocks.x: Every AI Chef Pro English edition is written in US English with US defaults: prices in dollars, sales tax added on top of the menu price, temperatures in °F, weights in pounds and ounces, and overtime after 40 hours a week. That is the starting point, not a limit. The numbers that change from one country to another live in editable input cells (usually the green ones), so a restaurant owner in Manchester, Toronto or Melbourne can make the kit their own in a few minutes.

This guide tells you **what to type in those cells** and **which words your team will use instead**. Work through it in this order: money and tax first, then wages and employer costs, then units and temperatures, and finally the labels you want to rename.

Add one line to any prompt, such as “Use British English, metric units and prices including VAT” (or GST for Australia, GST/HST for Canada).

**Renaming labels.** You can rename column headings and printed titles so they sound like your team (“rota”, “roster”, “stocktake”). Do not rename the values inside drop-down lists, such as units or categories: formulas look them up by their exact text.
The kits use the US word. If your guests and your team say it differently, this is the word to use on your menu, your prep lists and your rota.

blocks.x: **The entrée trap.** On a US menu, the entrée is the main course. In Australia, and on many British menus that use French terms, the entrée is the starter. If a kit says “Appetizer / Entrée” and you trade in Australia, relabel it “Entrée / Main” before you print anything, or guests will expect a full plate.

**Same everywhere.** “Back of house” (BOH: kitchen, dish area, storage) and “front of house” (FOH: dining room, bar, host stand) are understood in all four countries, and so are “covers” for guests served, “mise en place” and “prep list”. US kitchen slang such as “86” (sold out) travels less well: explain it to new staff.
Back-office words change more than kitchen words. The table below covers the ones that appear in the kits' tabs, reports and instructions.

blocks.x: Food cost % and GP % are two sides of one number

US and Canadian operators watch food cost %: what the plate costs as a share of the price. British operators talk about GP % (gross profit): what is left after the food cost. They always add up to 100%. A 30% food cost is a 70% GP.
The trap is tax. Always calculate either figure on the price **without** tax. In the UK and Australia the printed price includes tax, so take it out first:

x: **Net price** = printed price ÷ (1 + tax rate). Example, UK: a dish printed at 12.00 with 20% VAT has a net price of 12.00 ÷ 1.20 = 10.00.
**Food cost %** = plate cost ÷ net price. If the plate costs 3.00, food cost is 3.00 ÷ 10.00 = 30%, and **GP %** = 100% − 30% = 70%.
If you used the printed 12.00 by mistake, food cost would look like 25% and GP like 75%: five points better than reality.
Australia: GST is one-eleventh of a GST-inclusive price. A dish printed at 22.00 carries 2.00 of GST and a net price of 20.00.
US and Canada: the menu price is already net of tax, so use it as it is. Tips never count as sales.

blocks.x: In the Food Cost Kit, set the Tax rate cell and the kit does this for you; in the business plans, type the average check without tax.

Allergens you must declare

x: **UK:** for food that is not prepacked, you can give allergen information in any form (menu, chalkboard, information pack) or orally, with a clearly visible notice telling guests how to ask. Food prepacked on your premises for direct sale needs a label with the full ingredients list, allergens emphasized.
**Australia:** where food is unpackaged, allergen information must be displayed with the food or provided on request.

**US and Canada:** the lists above are labeling rules for packaged food; ask your health department or province what a restaurant must tell guests. The HACCP kit's matrix already holds all 14 UK allergens, which covers every country's list except Australia's rule to name each tree nut and each gluten cereal (wheat, barley, oats, rye) separately.

Minimum wage: where to look, not what to type

x: **US:** federal, state and sometimes city minimum wages all apply, and the employee gets the highest. Tipped-wage rules also vary by state. Check the Department of Labor's state table.
**UK:** the rate depends on the worker's age band and changes every April. Check the National Minimum Wage rates page on gov.uk.
**Canada:** each province and territory sets its own rate. Check your province's employment standards office.
**Australia:** the minimum for a cook, server or kitchen hand is the rate for their classification in the Hospitality Industry (General) Award, updated every July 1. Check the Fair Work Ombudsman.

The kits accept metric units next to US ones, but a few traps catch everyone: an ounce of weight is not a fluid ounce, and US pints and gallons are smaller than imperial ones. The factors below come from NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C, rounded where needed.
Formulas

x: **US volume:** 1 US fl oz = 29.5735 ml · 1 cup = 8 fl oz (about 237 ml) · 1 US pint = 16 fl oz (473 ml) · 1 US gallon = 128 fl oz = 3.785411784 L
**Imperial volume (UK):** 1 imperial gallon = 160 imperial fl oz (4.546 L) · 1 imperial pint = 20 imperial fl oz (568 ml) · 1 imperial fl oz = 28.41 ml

**Spoons:** 1 US tablespoon = 3 teaspoons (half a US fl oz, 14.79 ml) · 1 teaspoon about 5 ml. An Australian tablespoon is 20 ml (4 teaspoons) and an Australian metric cup is 250 ml: the kit's “tbsp” and “cup” are US measures, so type Australian measures in ml.
**Area:** 1 sq ft = 0.09290304 m² · 1 m² = 10.764 sq ft · **Distance:** 1 mile = 1.609344 km · 1 km = 0.6214 mile
